name: The Long Pour
description: A Shelf-born tradition observed over the 48-hour period of the winter solstice, rooted in the 2188 collapse of the Ward 3 municipal water reclamation system that left 200,000 Tier 1 residents without potable water for 31 days during a freeze event. The tradition centers on a shared meal built entirely from preserved, foraged, or traded food — nothing purchased from a corporate vendor — eaten by candlelight with an empty cup on the table for those who did not survive the freeze. Over time it has absorbed other grief: the empty cup is now set for anyone lost to poverty, corporate negligence, or street violence in the past year.
cultural_impact: The Long Pour is one of the most emotionally significant cultural observances on the Shelf, functioning simultaneously as a grief ritual, a food-sharing network, and an annual reaffirmation of mutual dependence over corporate supply chains. The tradition of building the meal from non-corporate sources has quietly sustained a parallel economy of Shelf food producers, foragers, and preservers that operates year-round in anticipation of the solstice meal.
key_figures: Tomás Achebe-Lindqvist (Ward 3 survivor, credited with first organized Long Pour meal)
Sable Oduya-Ferreira (Long Pour recipe archivist and oral historian)
Grandmother Kwon-Petrov (informal title given annually to the eldest Long Pour host in each ward)
locations: The Long Table (annual Ward 7 communal gathering, seats 800)
Rotating household and collective sites across all Shelf wards
story_hooks: This year's Long Pour meal in Ward 7 is being planned by someone who has quietly substituted a corporate food supplier for several ingredients and is covering it up — to a community that treats the purity of the meal as sacred.

The Ward 3 Community Hearth, the original Long Pour site, is scheduled for demolition by a corponation development project set to break ground the day after the solstice — and the community has 48 hours to decide how to respond.

A player character is invited to their first Long Pour and must navigate the ritual of the empty cup — only to recognize the name called for the cup as someone they were told died under very different circumstances.
origin_event: The 2188 Ward 3 Water Reclamation Collapse, in which infrastructure failure during a freeze event cut potable water to 200,000 Tier 1 residents for 31 days. Eighteen people died. Municipal authorities took 11 days to formally acknowledge the failure. Tomás Achebe-Lindqvist organized a shared meal from community stores on the 31st day, when water was restored, and named it the Long Pour.
tier_observations: Tier 1: The full ritual — preserved/foraged/traded meal, empty cup, reading of names, 48-hour candlelight; the most intimate and significant holiday in the Shelf calendar. Tier 2: Many with Shelf roots observe the full tradition; others adopt the shared meal aspect and the empty cup without the non-corporate food restriction. Tier 3: A small number observe it as a heritage practice; more common among Tier 3 residents with recent Shelf family history. Tier 4-5: Entirely unknown; the solstice is marked by corporate-sponsored winter events and Spire galas.
